pos: noun phrase, in ‘by the skin of my teeth’ (only just, narrowly)
etymology: The phrase is word for word from the King James Version of Job 19:20: "I am escaped with the skin of my teeth." English keeps it in the idiom by the skin of my teeth, meaning by the narrowest margin. The key word is skin (Oxford English Dictionary).
biblical_def: To escape by the skin of my teeth is to escape by the smallest possible margin. The words are Job’s. Stripped of his children, his goods and his health, and mocked by his friends, he describes how little is left of him: "My bone cleaveth to my skin and to my flesh, and I am escaped with the skin of my teeth" (Job 19:20). He had come through with almost nothing. The Christian observation: the same chapter does not end in despair. A few verses later Job makes one of the great confessions of the Old Testament: "For I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth" (Job 19:25), and "yet in my flesh shall I see God" (Job 19:26). The man who had barely escaped still had the one thing that mattered.
webster_summary: Only just, by the narrowest margin; from Job’s complaint, "I am escaped with the skin of my teeth" (Job 19:20), spoken in the chapter where he confesses, "I know that my redeemer liveth" (Job 19:25).
webster_full: SKIN OF MY TEETH, n. phr. In by the skin of my teeth: barely, with nothing to spare. From Job 19:20 (KJV).
Scripture setting: Job, reduced to almost nothing, who still confesses a living Redeemer (Job 19:25–26).
scriptures: My bone cleaveth to my skin and to my flesh, and I am escaped with the skin of my teeth.
For I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth:
And though after my skin worms destroy this body, yet in my flesh shall I see God:
corruption_summary: The idiom keeps Job’s narrow escape and forgets the Redeemer he confessed in the same chapter.
corruption_paragraphs: Men use the phrase for a close call: a test passed, a deadline met, a wreck avoided. It has become a light thing. In Job it was not light. He had lost nearly everything, and his friends were accusing him.

The chapter that gives us the phrase also gives one of the clearest hopes of resurrection in the Old Testament (Job 19:25–26). A man may come through with almost nothing and still have everything, if his Redeemer lives.
roots_summary: skin (OED) → "I am escaped with the skin of my teeth" (Job 19:20, KJV) → idiom by the skin of my teeth.
roots_lines: Job 19:20: Job’s description of his wasted body
Job 19:25: "I know that my redeemer liveth"
Modern idiom: by the skin of my teeth, barely
usage: "We made the last flight out by the skin of our teeth."
I am escaped with the skin of my teeth. (Job 19:20).
For I know that my redeemer liveth. (Job 19:25).

pos: noun phrase (one responsible for another’s welfare)
etymology: The phrase is word for word from the King James Version of Gen 4:9, Cain’s answer to God: "Am I my brother’s keeper?" The key word is keeper (Oxford English Dictionary).
biblical_def: To say I am not my brother’s keeper is to deny any duty for another man’s welfare. The words come from the first murder. When the LORD asked Cain, "Where is Abel thy brother?" Cain answered, "I know not: Am I my brother’s keeper?" (Gen 4:9). He had just killed him. God answered with a question of his own: "What hast thou done? the voice of thy brother’s blood crieth unto me from the ground" (Gen 4:10). The Christian observation: Cain’s question was a lie and a dodge, and the rest of Scripture answers it. John points back to him: "Not as Cain, who was of that wicked one, and slew his brother" (1Jn 3:12). Then he gives the Christian answer: "Hereby perceive we the love of God, because he laid down his life for us: and we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren" (1Jn 3:16).
webster_summary: One responsible for another’s good; from Cain’s evasion, "Am I my brother’s keeper?" (Gen 4:9), answered in the gospel by love that lays down its life for the brethren (1Jn 3:16).
webster_full: MY BROTHER’S KEEPER, n. phr. One who is answerable for another’s welfare; usually in the denial I am not my brother’s keeper. From Gen 4:9 (KJV).
Scripture sense: Cain’s question, asked to hide a murder, which God did not accept.
scriptures: Gen 4:9
And the LORD said unto Cain, Where is Abel thy brother? And he said, I know not: Am I my brother's keeper?
Gen 4:10
And he said, What hast thou done? the voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto me from the ground.
Not as Cain, who was of that wicked one, and slew his brother. And wherefore slew he him? Because his own works were evil, and his brother's righteous.
Hereby perceive we the love of God, because he laid down his life for us: and we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren.
corruption_summary: Men still quote Cain to excuse themselves from one another. Scripture treats his question as the evasion of a murderer, and it answers him with Christ’s love for the brethren.
corruption_paragraphs: "I’m not my brother’s keeper" is said as if it were common sense. Mind your own business, look after your own house. In Genesis it is the first lie told to cover the first murder.

The gospel does not leave the question open. Christ laid down his life for us, and "we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren" (1Jn 3:16). A man who will not watch over his brother has more in common with Cain than he thinks.
roots_summary: keeper (OED) → "Am I my brother’s keeper?" (Gen 4:9, KJV) → idiom for responsibility for another.
roots_lines: Gen 4:9: Cain’s answer to the LORD after killing Abel
Gen 4:10: the voice of Abel’s blood
1Jn 3:16: the Christian answer, love that lays down its life
usage: "He called the men together and told them each was his brother’s keeper."
We ought to lay down our lives for the brethren. (1Jn 3:16).

pos: noun phrase (work done for love, not for pay)
etymology: The phrase is word for word from the King James Version, which uses it twice: "your work of faith, and labour of love" (1Th 1:3) and "your work and labour of love, which ye have shewed toward his name" (Heb 6:10). The key word is labour (Oxford English Dictionary).
biblical_def: A labour of love is work done gladly for its own sake or for someone loved, without thought of pay. The phrase comes from Paul. He thanked God for the Thessalonians, "Remembering without ceasing your work of faith, and labour of love, and patience of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ" (1Th 1:3). Hebrews uses it again: "God is not unrighteous to forget your work and labour of love, which ye have shewed toward his name, in that ye have ministered to the saints" (Heb 6:10). The Christian observation: in Scripture the labour of love is service to Christ’s people, and God remembers it. It is the fruit of faith, the "faith which worketh by love" (Gal 5:6), not a way of earning anything.
webster_summary: Work done for love rather than pay; from "labour of love" (1Th 1:3; Heb 6:10), the service of believers that God does not forget.
webster_full: LABOUR OF LOVE, n. phr. Work undertaken for love or devotion rather than for gain. From 1Th 1:3 and Heb 6:10 (KJV). The American spelling is labor of love.
Scripture sense: the ministry of believers to the saints, which God remembers (Heb 6:10).
scriptures: Remembering without ceasing your work of faith, and labour of love, and patience of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ, in the sight of God and our Father;
Heb 6:10
For God is not unrighteous to forget your work and labour of love, which ye have shewed toward his name, in that ye have ministered to the saints, and do minister.
Gal 5:6
For in Jesus Christ neither circumcision availeth any thing, nor uncircumcision; but faith which worketh by love.
corruption_summary: Common use makes a labour of love any hobby a man enjoys. Scripture means work done for Christ’s people, out of faith, that God himself remembers.
corruption_paragraphs: Today a restored truck or a hand-built boat is called a labour of love, and the phrase means little more than "he enjoyed it." There is nothing wrong with that. But the phrase once named something weightier.

Paul and the writer to the Hebrews used it for the work of believers serving one another in Christ’s name (Heb 6:10). It grows from faith (Gal 5:6), and it is often unseen and unpaid. God does not forget it.
roots_summary: labour (OED) → "labour of love" (1Th 1:3; Heb 6:10, KJV) → idiom for unpaid, devoted work.
roots_lines: 1Th 1:3: work of faith, labour of love, patience of hope
Heb 6:10: God does not forget the labour of love
usage: "Rebuilding the old chapel was a labour of love for the whole congregation."
Your work of faith, and labour of love. (1Th 1:3).
God is not unrighteous to forget your work and labour of love. (Heb 6:10).

etymology: The phrase is word for word from the King James Version of Isa 65:5, the boast of a rebellious people: "Stand by thyself, come not near to me; for I am holier than thou." The key word is holy (Oxford English Dictionary).
biblical_def: To be holier than thou is to look down on others from a height of your own goodness. The words are a boast God condemns. Through Isaiah he describes a rebellious people who keep their own rituals and say to others, "Stand by thyself, come not near to me; for I am holier than thou." God’s verdict follows at once: "These are a smoke in my nose, a fire that burneth all the day" (Isa 65:5). Christ drew the same man in the Pharisee who "stood and prayed thus with himself, God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are" (Luk 18:11). The Christian observation: the phrase does not mock holiness. It mocks the pride that pretends to it. True holiness is a gift of grace, and it makes a man humble, not proud.
webster_summary: Smugly self-righteous; from the boast God condemns, "I am holier than thou" (Isa 65:5), the spirit of the Pharisee who thanked God he was not as other men (Luk 18:11).
webster_full: HOLIER-THAN-THOU, a. Affecting moral superiority; sanctimonious. From Isa 65:5 (KJV).
Scripture sense: the boast of a proud, rebellious people, which God calls "a smoke in my nose".
scriptures: Isa 65:5
Which say, Stand by thyself, come not near to me; for I am holier than thou. These are a smoke in my nose, a fire that burneth all the day.
The Pharisee stood and prayed thus with himself, God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even as this publican.
corruption_summary: The world now calls any moral conviction "holier than thou." Scripture condemns the proud boast, not the pursuit of holiness itself.
corruption_paragraphs: The charge "holier than thou" is thrown at anyone who holds a moral line, as though conviction itself were pride. That turns Isaiah upside down. God condemned a people who were not holy at all but claimed to be, and who used the claim to keep others away.

Scripture still commands holiness. The cure for the holier-than-thou spirit is not to give up holiness. It is to remember that holiness is God’s gift, that the Pharisee went home unjustified (Luk 18:11), and that the man who knows his own sin cannot look down on his brother.
roots_summary: holy (OED) → "for I am holier than thou" (Isa 65:5, KJV) → idiom for smug self-righteousness.
roots_lines: Isa 65:5: the boast of a rebellious people
usage: "His holier-than-thou tone lost him the room."
Stand by thyself, come not near to me; for I am holier than thou. (Isa 65:5).
God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are. (Luk 18:11).
